tur50-1: According to a Cochrane review of 13 trials and 839 people, aerobic exercise probably improves quality of life and may slightly improve pain and day-to-day function (low to moderate certainty of evidence). In a US trial of 226 people with fibromyalgia, tai chi done once or twice a week gave similar or greater benefit than aerobic exercise. Tai chi for 24 weeks was more effective than a 12-week programme; doing it twice a week brought no significant extra benefit over once a week.
tur50-2: In people with severe pain or sleep problems, a doctor may start medication if they consider it necessary.
tur50-3: In one 58-person trial within a Cochrane review of nine trials (395 people), acupuncture added to standard treatment with medication and exercise reduced pain by about 3 points on a 0–10 scale (moderate-quality evidence). Acupuncture with mild electrical current through the needles also reduced pain somewhat compared with sham treatment; manual acupuncture showed no such difference. The effect lasted about a month and was not maintained at six months. The evidence is low to moderate quality; side effects were mild and short-lived.

tur50-5: Not every shaking hand is Parkinson's. Parkinson's tremor is usually seen when the hand is at rest; in essential tremor, one of the most common types, the hand shakes while doing something. A neurologist makes the distinction by examination; see one if your tremor is getting worse over time.
tur50-6: Things change once movement starts to return. According to a Cochrane review of physical treatments (12 trials, 872 people), tailored facial exercises may improve facial function, particularly in moderate and long-lasting palsy; the quality of evidence is low. In the same review, a benefit of electrical stimulation could not be shown; the evidence was insufficient.
tur50-7: A Cochrane review of six trials (537 people) could not reach a conclusion on whether acupuncture works for facial palsy because the trials were of inadequate quality; no harmful side effects were reported in any of the trials. Facial Palsy UK advises avoiding acupuncture with electrical stimulation through the needles in the early phase.
tur50-8: Most people's symptoms start to improve within a few weeks and clear up within six months; in some people it can take longer or leave lasting effects. Steroid treatment started within the first 72 hours increases the chance of full recovery. If your symptoms are not getting better after three weeks, see your doctor again.
tur50-9: The Cochrane review included four trials of electrical stimulation (313 people). In one of them (86 people), electrical stimulation was no better than sham treatment for recovery at six months; in another, low-quality trial reporting at three months (56 people), recovery was worse. The review concluded that the evidence is insufficient to decide whether electrical stimulation works.
